The theory of the five elements (Wu Xing) describes five dynamic categories: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water. The word "element" is easily misleading: in Chinese, xing means rather "movement" or "phase." Each element designates a pattern of transformation, not a physical substance. Wood is associated with growth and expansion, Fire with maximum activity, Earth with transformation and balance, Metal with contraction and clarification, Water with rest and conservation.

Cupping creates a vacuum that gently lifts the skin and tissues. A distinction is made between dry cupping (static, gliding) and wet cupping (hijama), where small superficial incisions are made and a little blood is drawn. Wet cupping carries a risk of infection, including transmission of blood-borne viruses, if the instruments are not sterile, so it should only be done by professionals with strict hygiene. Yin and Yang are a pair of complementary opposites. Yang is associated with activity, heat, the exterior, the upper part and the back of the body; Yin with rest, coolness, the interior, the lower part and the front. Zang-Fu is the traditional name for the internal "organs" in TCM. The Zang are the "full" or yin organs (Liver, Heart, Spleen, Lung, Kidney, plus the Pericardium), considered storehouses of vital substances. The Fu are the "hollow" or yang organs (Gallbladder, Small Intestine, Stomach, Large Intestine, Urinary Bladder and the Triple Burner), which receive, transform and eliminate. By convention, we capitalize the names so as not to confuse them with the anatomical organs.

In TCM, Qi (pronounced roughly "chee") is the central idea. It is described as a vital activity that moves, warms, defends and transforms. It is not a measurable substance in the physical sense, but an explanatory concept: a scheme by which traditional physicians organized observations about energy, digestion, breathing or resistance to illness. When we say "in the TCM tradition, Qi is blocked," we are describing a model, not a structure we have seen under a microscope.
